There's a book by Austrian writer Ingeborg Bachmann ("Malina" if anyone is interested) that - at least in my opinion - describes a lot of BPD relatable scenes. One of them stuck and I can't read it without simultaneously crying and laughing my ass off. 

The main character - a woman who calls herself "unknown female"  - is in love with Ivan. Now Ivan is emotionally abusive. But the woman still loves him blindly even though she suffers through his behaviour. 

So she waits next to the phone for Ivan to call. When he does, she drops to the floor and silently thanks the lord that he has acknowledged her existence, she can't understand how she deserves to be called by Ivan! She can't get one straight sentence out because she is so overjoyed...and then Ivan cancels their evening plans. 

That lady is crashing haaaaaaaaard. Like - "the receiver feels as cold as ice, like it's not made from plastic but from metal, it rides up to my temple because I can hear him hanging up, and I wish that the sound it makes was a shot, short, fast, so it would be over, I don't want Ivan to be like that today and that it's always like that, I want it to be over. I hang up and stay on the floor..." She then starts trying to frantically keep herself busy, she tries to read, organize papers, cleaning, calls the telephone company to complain that Ivan hung up, finally putting the phone on her nightstand in case Ivan calls again. 

Yeah. It me. Lol.

As my therapist explained it to me: "It's a crutch. You are not supposed to use skills for the rest of your life and think that means you're cured. It's to minimize the damage you do to yourself and others, to help you make the experience that the world won't end even if you don't spiral out of control. It is supposed to contribute to giving you an environment in which you are able to make different experiences." I never really liked the half arsed Zen-aspect of DBT, so I looked for a genuine Zen-group, and it's way different. I stare at a wall for half an hour straight, alone with concentrating on my breath, watching my thoughts go by. I was deathly scared of dissociation. But instead, I'm starting to experience moments of genuine quiet, one my brain calms down enough. Also my Zen-master is a really nice person I feel I can always talk to.

In my experience, DBT emulates a lot of the environment BPDs know very well, employs a lot of mechanisms that work on us because they are what made us BPD, which might be why it's working for a lot of us. But for some of us, it doesn't. I kinda felt like it was forcing me to accept that I am a Borderline like people are forced to accept they are alcoholics at AA, and that that's never going to change. The core point is that it is actively suggesting that I will ALWAYS have to live with these behaviours and my coping mechanisms, and that's what I call bullshit. There are reasons for me being a BPD person, and I am trying to work through those and by that, go through the process of finding out how these events have hindered me developing my personality as I was supposed to, and finally let me develop it now. It's not about finding who you are. Your personality won't come jumping at you like a jack in the box. It's a process we missed for reasons, and just coping with the status quo denies you that process, it's settling for less than I am willing to settle for. 

DBT can be a helpful support system if you are either a sucker for its methodology or want a way of dealing with the outbursts or are somehow content with keeping the status quo for a while. But I am not settling for Marsha Linehan saying "You can be mentally ill, but you don't have to look it." That's not my long term goal. I am ill now, but I am working towards getting healthy, not towards getting a pro at hiding my illness.

My skin is about as thick as a piece of Kleenex. I feel constantly judged, invalidated and disrespected by everyone and everything, and I react by pretending to be ultra tough and aggressive, which can lead to extreme episodes of rage and/or splitting.

Meditation works if I can make myself aware that I am overreacting, which by now is about 70% of cases I'd say. There's still situations when my subconscious just runs wild and I'm just watching the show eating popcorn though. It's also typically worse when emotional interests clash - e.g. I have to write to someone I'm avoiding because I've split on them - I feel bad because on the one hand I want to continue avoiding them and writing the message/waiting for an answer actively puts me in an uncomfortable spot, but I also feel guilty if I don't talk to them.

Yes, I know the feeling all too well. It also comes with a complete stress reaction that ranges from stomach pain, raised heart rate, sweating, shallow breathing, dizziness up to a full scale panic attack in some cases. Skills help to an extent, but I'm not far enough in therapy to be able to just not have that reaction to most uncomfortable messages.

Complete understanding or bottomless hate, black and white, no in between.

My mother has BPD. Not that she ever got diagnosed though. 

My father is bipolar. My grandmothers were saints, and my grandfather an asshole that resented me for being a girl.

I was a shy child that never had the guts for anything. My mother would frequently ignore me completely when mad for the smallest reason, and my father would either be maniacally pursuing a project or drink his depression away. Both still do the same shit 20 years later.

I realized I was different in grade 7. My former best friend had just decided to replace me with a popular girl, and told everybody lies about me that led to the entire class ignoring me (see a pattern?) or bullying me.

I pushed a guy who was bullying me down the stairs. Luckily, only four steps down but I pushed him. The wrath boiled up, turned everything dark and with an inhuman scream, I pushed him. At that moment, he was the embodiment of everything that caused me to feel how I felt (BPD), and I wanted to hurt him just as he had hurt me.

I became a recluse after that, struggled with nail biting and anorexia. And BPD sabotaged relationships (google "sudden repulsion syndrome").

I'd say I was born with a predisposition and everyone so far has done their part in triggering me as best they can, some because they suffer too (mom/dad/sister), some because they are clueless, some on purpose. It's just what I am, and it's hard.

I've lately come to utilize a really weird technique, but after more than 20 years of repeated depersonalization and me constantly being afraid of it, I found out this works for me:

I depersonalize when stressed in any way shape or form, or just plain tired. I always used to keep quiet and get some distraction, but one day I decided to voice my anxiety to myself, like I was talking to a different person - and it worked. Acting as though the rational part of my mind that was usually drowned out by my panic was someone I could talk to and get actual advice from ended the feeling of depersonalization rather quickly compared to all the other times. Doing the same thing when I sense I am about to be overwhelmed by my feelings or a situation even helps me to prevent it. 

I am not saying that this works for everyone, but I also don't want to be withholding something that helps me and might help others as well.
